explain: Values: int, float, str, bool, None, list [ ] and dict { }. Everything is a value (an object).
example: Lists and dicts are what most programs store.
remember: Python's six: number, decimal, text, yes/no, nothing, list, dict.

syntax:
name = "Po"
count = 0
count += 1
print(name, count)
explain: Variables: a name = a value. No let or const; just =.
remember: Name on the left, value on the right.

explain: Blocks: a line ending in : starts a block, and the indented lines under it are inside it. Indentation is the grammar (no { }).
example: if, for, while, def, class all use : + indent.
remember: Colon opens, indent holds, un-indent closes.

explain: Functions: def name(parameters): then an indented block; return sends a value back.

syntax:
word = "hello"
print(word.upper(), word.count("l"), len(word))
explain: Everything is an object with methods you reach with a dot. Some tools are plain functions (len, print).
remember: Dot = "ask the value to do something".

explain: A class is a block of functions (methods). self is the object itself.
example: Making your own kinds of objects.
remember: class = a block of defs that share self.

syntax: print([n * 2 for n in range(5) if n % 2 == 0])
explain: A list comprehension is a for loop and an if squeezed inside [ ].
example: Building a list in one line.
remember: [ what for x in where if test ]

syntax:
with open("note.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("hi")
print(open("note.txt").read())
explain: with is a block that opens something and closes it for you at the end.

syntax:
name = "Ada"
print(f"Hello, {name}!")
explain: A variable, and an f-string that puts values inside { }.
example: Printing a friendly message with a user name.

explain: Python uses a colon and 4 spaces of indentation instead of { }.

syntax:
for i in range(3):
    print(i)
explain: range(3) gives 0, 1, 2. The loop body is indented.
example: Repeating a task a set number of times.

explain: def makes a function. return sends the result back.
example: Reusable steps, like cleaning a line of text.

syntax:
fruits = ["apple", "banana"]
fruits.append("cherry")
print(fruits[0], len(fruits))
explain: A list in [ ]. append adds to the end, [0] is the first item, len counts.
example: A shopping list or a list of file names.

explain: Values stored under keys. get gives a default instead of crashing.
example: Settings, or one row of data.

syntax:
squares = [n * n for n in range(5)]
evens = [n for n in range(10) if n % 2 == 0]
print(squares, evens)
explain: Build a new list in one line, optionally keeping only some items.
example: Turning a list of prices into a list with tax.

explain: A class is a blueprint. __init__ runs when you make one; self is the object.
example: Modelling things in a game: players, enemies, items.

syntax:
import random
from datetime import date

print(random.randint(1, 6))
print(date.today())
explain: import loads ready-made modules that come with Python.
example: Dice rolls, dates, reading files, web requests.

syntax:
name = "Ada"
age = 36
print(f"{name} is {age}. Next year: {age + 1}")
explain: f-strings put values inside text with {}.
After : you can format: 2 decimals, right-align in 5 spaces, commas.

syntax:
name = input("Your name: ")
age = int(input("Your age: "))
print(name, age)
explain: input() reads text typed by the user. int() turns it into a number.

syntax: print(int("5") + 1, str(5) + "!", float("2.5"), type(5))
explain: Convert between numbers and text. type() tells you what something is.
elif checks the next condition when the first is false.

syntax:
x = 5
print(0 < x < 10, x == 5 and x != 6, not True)
explain: Python can chain comparisons. and, or, not combine conditions.
example: Checking a number is in range.

syntax:
n = 3
while n > 0:
    print(n)
    n -= 1
print("Go!")
explain: while repeats as long as the condition is true.
continue skips to the next round, break stops the loop.
example: Stopping when you find what you need.

syntax:
for i in range(0, 10, 3):
    print(i)
explain: range(start, stop, step). Stop is not included.

syntax:
for i, fruit in enumerate(["apple", "kiwi"], start=1):
    print(i, fruit)
explain: enumerate gives the position and the item together.

syntax:
names = ["Ada", "Bo"]
ages = [36, 25]
for name, age in zip(names, ages):
    print(name, age)
explain: zip walks through two lists side by side.

syntax:
nums = [3, 1, 2]
nums.append(4)
nums.insert(0, 9)
nums.remove(1)
last = nums.pop()
nums.sort()
print(nums, last, len(nums))
explain: Add, insert, remove, pop and sort change the list itself.

syntax:
letters = ["a", "b", "c", "d", "e"]
print(letters[0], letters[-1], letters[1:3], letters[::-1])
explain: [i] picks one, [-1] is the last, [a:b] slices, [::-1] reverses.

syntax:
print(len([1, 2]), sum([1, 2, 3]), min([4, 2]), max([4, 2]))
print(sorted(["b", "a"]), sorted([1, 3, 2], reverse=True))
explain: Built-in helpers for lists. sorted makes a new sorted list.

syntax: print(any(n > 2 for n in [1, 3]), all(n > 0 for n in [1, 3]))
explain: any: at least one is true. all: every one is true.
example: Checking if any task is late.

syntax:
point = (3, 4)
x, y = point
a, b = 1, 2
a, b = b, a
print(x, y, a, b)
explain: A tuple is a list that can't change. Unpacking assigns several variables at once.
A set keeps only unique values. & is "in both", | is "in either".
get returns a default instead of crashing. items() gives key-value pairs.
A dict comprehension builds a dictionary in one line.

syntax:
s = "  Hello, World  "
print(s.strip().lower(), s.replace("World", "Ada"), "a,b,c".split(","), "-".join(["a", "b"]))
explain: Clean up, change case, replace, split into a list, join a list into text.
example: Cleaning data from a CSV file.

syntax:
s = "python"
print(s.upper(), s.startswith("py"), s.find("th"), s.count("o"), s[0:2])
explain: Text has many helpers. Text can be sliced like a list.
greeting="Hi" is a default. You can also pass arguments by name.
*args collects extra values into a tuple, **kwargs collects named ones into a dict.

syntax:
square = lambda n: n * n
print(square(4))
print(sorted(["kiwi", "fig", "apple"], key=len))
explain: lambda is a tiny one-line function. key= tells sorted what to sort by.
example: Sorting by length, by date, by price.

syntax: print(list(map(str.upper, ["a", "b"])), list(filter(lambda n: n > 1, [1, 2, 3])))
explain: map changes every item, filter keeps some. Comprehensions often read better.
try runs code; except handles a kind of error; finally always runs.
raise stops the function with an error.

syntax:
with open("notes.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("line 1\nline 2\n")
with open("notes.txt") as f:
    for line in f:
        print(line.strip())
explain: with open closes the file for you. "w" writes, "a" appends, no letter reads.

syntax:
import json
with open("data.json", "w") as f:
    json.dump({"count": 1}, f)
with open("data.json") as f:
    print(json.load(f))
explain: json saves Python data to a file and loads it back.

syntax:
from pathlib import Path
p = Path("demo.txt")
p.write_text("hello")
print(p.exists(), p.read_text(), p.suffix, list(Path(".").glob("*.txt")))
explain: pathlib makes working with files and folders easy.
example: Finding all .txt files in a folder.

explain: __str__ decides what print() shows for your object.
example: Readable output for your own types.

explain: class Cat(Animal) inherits from Animal and can replace its methods.
@dataclass writes __init__, printing and == for you.
yield gives values one at a time instead of building a whole list.
example: Reading huge files line by line.

explain: A decorator wraps a function to add behavior. @name applies it.
example: Timing functions, checking logins (Flask uses these).

explain: Type hints say what types are expected. Python doesn't enforce them; editors use them.
example: Catching mistakes early in big projects.

explain: This code runs only when the file is run directly, not when it's imported.
example: Scripts that are also importable modules.

syntax:
from math import sqrt, pi
import datetime
print(sqrt(16), round(pi, 2), datetime.date.today())
explain: from x import y takes just what you need from a module.

syntax:
import random
print(random.choice(["rock", "paper", "scissors"]), random.randint(1, 6))
nums = [1, 2, 3]
random.shuffle(nums)
print(nums)
explain: choice picks one, randint picks a whole number, shuffle mixes a list.

syntax:
from collections import Counter
print(Counter("hello world").most_common(2))
explain: Counter counts how many times each thing appears.
example: Most common words in a text.

explain: None means "no value". Check it with is None.

syntax:
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install requests
pip freeze > requirements.txt
explain: A venv keeps each project's packages separate. pip installs packages.
